The question of whether animals should be used in research is deeply contested, with strong arguments on both sides. Pro-research sources argue that animal research is scientifically necessary and legally required. According to Stanford University, "animals must continue to play a critical role in helping researchers test potential new drugs and medical treatments for effectiveness and safety," because no substitute has been found for a living, whole-organ system [d1]. The NIH similarly states that "animals have unique and important roles in biomedical and behavioral research" and that "many medical advances that enhance the lives of humans are developed from research studies with animals" [d3]. The U.S. Government's own principles affirm that "the development of knowledge necessary for the improvement of the health and well-being of humans as well as other animals requires in vivo experimentation with a wide variety of animal species" [d6], and the American Physiological Society notes that scientists use animals "when there is no alternative and it is impractical or unethical to study humans" [d2].

On the opposing side, critics argue that animal research is both ethically wrong and scientifically unreliable. A peer-reviewed PMC article concludes that "animal experiments, no matter the species used or the type of disease research undertaken, are highly unreliable—and they have too little predictive value to justify the resultant risks of harms for humans," because species differences far outweigh similarities [d8]. Cruelty Free International reports that "92% of drugs fail in human clinical trials despite appearing safe and effective in animal tests," and that using common lab animals "provides statistically little useful insight" into human drug safety [d12]. From an ethical standpoint, one source argues that "animals should not be used in research or to test the safety of products" because their basic moral rights are violated when they cannot consent to participation [d7]. PETA further contends that animal experiments "prolong the suffering of humans waiting for effective cures because the results mislead experimenters and squander precious money, time, and other resources" [d9], and that modern alternatives such as human tissue-based research and computational models "have the potential to be more reliable, more precise, less expensive, and more humane" [d10]. The EU has taken a middle-ground institutional position, setting "a final goal of full replacement of all animals used for scientific and educational purposes" while permitting regulated use in the interim under the Three Rs principle [d4].
